title: Alexander Graham Bell, Teacher of Sound
summary: Alexander Graham Bell grew up in Scotland in a family that studied how people speak. He became a teacher of deaf students in Boston, and at night he tinkered with wires, magnets and tuned steel reeds. Then, on a hot June day in 1875, a stuck reed made a twang that changed everything.

sections.heading: A Family Obsessed with Voices
paragraphs: Alexander Bell was born on 3 March 1847 in Edinburgh, Scotland, in a family home on South Charlotte Street. Yes, at first he was just Alexander Bell. He was named after his grandfather, and his family called him "Aleck". When he was 10, he asked for a middle name like his two brothers had, and on his 11th birthday he adopted "Graham", after Alexander Graham, a Canadian who knew his father.

If any family was going to produce an inventor of the telephone, it was probably this one, because the Bells were experts in the human voice. Aleck's grandfather, also named Alexander Bell, taught elocution, the art of speaking clearly and expressively, and helped people who stammered. His father, Alexander Melville Bell, was a famous teacher of speech and a phonetician, a scientist who studies the sounds of language. He wrote books on speaking that were used in schools for decades. Words, mouths, tongues and voices were discussed at the Bell dinner table the way some families talk about football.

Aleck's mother, Eliza Grace Symonds Bell, was a talented painter of miniature portraits and a gifted pianist. She was also hard of hearing, and her hearing got worse as Aleck grew older, until she was deaf. She used an ear trumpet, a horn-shaped tube held to the ear to collect sound. Aleck found his own way to talk with her: instead of shouting, he spoke in a low, clear voice very close to her forehead, so that she could feel the vibrations of his voice through her head. He also learned to use finger spelling with her. Many historians believe that growing up with a deaf mother helped make Aleck deeply curious about how sound travels and how people hear.

He was a lively, inventive boy. When he was about 12, he was playing at a neighbour's flour mill and saw how hard it was to remove the husks from wheat grains. He came up with a simple machine, using rotating paddles and a nail brush, that did the job. It was used at the mill for years. Aleck also loved music, played the piano by ear and was a brilliant mimic who could imitate voices and sounds.

sections.heading: Visible Speech and a Talking Dog
paragraphs: In the 1860s Aleck's father worked on his greatest project. He wanted a way to write down any sound any human could make, in any language or accent. Ordinary letters are not good at this. Think of how differently the letters "ough" sound in "though", "through" and "cough". Melville Bell's answer was a system he called Visible Speech, published in 1867 in a book called "Visible Speech: The Science of Universal Alphabetics".

Visible Speech did not use normal letters at all. Each symbol was a little picture of what your mouth does. Curved shapes showed the position of the tongue, other marks showed whether the lips were open or rounded, and a line showed whether the voice box was buzzing. If you learned to read these symbols, you could pronounce a word you had never heard, in a language you did not know, just by following the instructions for your mouth.

Aleck and his brothers helped demonstrate the system. Their father would send the boys out of the room. A volunteer from the audience would then make some strange sound, perhaps a phrase in a foreign language, a sneeze, or a regional accent, and Melville Bell would write it down in Visible Speech. When the boys came back in, they would read the symbols and reproduce the sound so exactly that audiences were amazed. It was a bit like a magic trick, but it was really science.

Melville Bell soon realized Visible Speech could help deaf people. Someone who cannot hear cannot copy speech by listening, but they could learn from symbols showing what to do with their lips, tongue and throat. This became one of the main tools Aleck used later as a teacher. (Over time, other teaching methods replaced Visible Speech, because it was complicated to learn.)

The Bell boys also had fun experimenting with speech themselves. After seeing a speaking machine built by the scientist Charles Wheatstone, Aleck and his older brother Melville (called "Melly") built their own talking head, with movable lips and tongue and a throat made from tin. When they blew air through it with a bellows, it could produce a sound like "Ma-ma", and Aleck later remembered that neighbours came out to look for the crying baby. Aleck also trained the family's Skye terrier, Trouve, to growl steadily while he moved the dog's mouth and throat with his hands. According to Bell's own memory, the result sounded a bit like "How are you, Grandmamma?" It was a silly experiment, but notice what he was doing: studying how shapes of the mouth turn a plain buzz into words.

sections.heading: A Young Teacher and a Lucky Mistake
paragraphs: Aleck went to the Royal High School in Edinburgh but was not a star pupil and left at 15. He then spent a year in London with his grandfather, who treated him like a young adult and encouraged his love of learning. At just 16 he became a pupil-teacher of elocution and music at Weston House Academy in Elgin, in the north of Scotland, teaching boys not much younger than himself while studying Latin and Greek. Later he studied at the University of Edinburgh and at University College London, though he did not finish a degree, and he taught at schools in Bath and London, including teaching deaf children.

He also kept experimenting. As a teenager he began studying how vowel sounds are made, using tuning forks held in front of his mouth to listen to the different pitches that make up each vowel. When he wrote about this to a speech expert, Alexander Ellis, he learned that the great German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz had already done similar work. Helmholtz had used electromagnets to make tuning forks vibrate and combine into vowel-like sounds.

Here comes one of the most famous mistakes in invention history. Bell could not read German well. Looking at Helmholtz's book, he got the wrong idea that Helmholtz had sent vowel sounds along a wire by electricity. Helmholtz had done no such thing. But Bell later said that this misunderstanding gave him confidence: if a famous scientist could send vowels electrically, then surely speech could travel along a wire too. Sometimes believing something is possible is what keeps an inventor going.

There was also great sadness in these years. Tuberculosis, a lung infection that was a leading cause of death in the 1800s, struck the family. Aleck's younger brother Edward died of it in 1867, and his older brother Melly in May 1870. Aleck himself was thin and unwell, and his parents feared he would be next. Melville Bell made a big decision: the family would leave Britain for a healthier life in Canada.

sections.heading: A New Home Above the Grand River
paragraphs: In the summer of 1870, Aleck, his parents and Melly's widow crossed the Atlantic. According to the City of Brantford, they arrived in August 1870 and settled on a small farm on a hill called Tutelo Heights, just outside Brantford, Ontario. The house, now known as the Bell Homestead, still stands and is a museum and a National Historic Site of Canada.

Aleck was 23 and in poor health when he arrived. The fresh country air, rest and walks did him good. He liked to sit on a slope above the Grand River, a spot he called his "dreaming place", and think. He turned a carriage house into a workshop. He also became interested in the language of the Mohawk people living nearby on the Six Nations reserve. He learned some Mohawk and wrote down its sounds using Visible Speech, and he was honoured by the community for this work.

In his Brantford workshop Bell was already mixing music and electricity. He adapted a melodeon, a small reed organ pumped with the feet, so that it could send musical notes along a wire by electricity. It was a small experiment, but it shows where his mind was heading: toward tones, reeds and electric currents, the same ingredients that would soon fill his Boston workroom.

After about eight months, Aleck was healthy again, and an opportunity arrived from the United States. A school for deaf children in Boston wanted someone to teach Visible Speech to its teachers. They had first asked his father, who suggested Aleck go instead. In April 1871 Aleck moved to Boston. For the next several years he lived and worked in the United States but returned to Brantford in the summers. That back-and-forth matters, because some of his most important telephone thinking happened on those visits home.

sections.heading: Teacher of the Deaf in Boston
paragraphs: Boston in the 1870s was a booming city of universities, factories, publishers and inventors. Bell began at the Boston School for Deaf Mutes (the word "mute" is no longer used this way, and today the school is called the Horace Mann School for the Deaf). Its principal, Sarah Fuller, was a pioneer in teaching deaf children to speak. Bell trained her teachers to use Visible Speech, and then repeated his training at schools in Hartford, Connecticut, and Northampton, Massachusetts. His results impressed people, and his reputation grew fast.

What did a lesson look like? Imagine a classroom with a large chart of Visible Speech symbols on the wall. Bell would point to a symbol and show a child where to place the lips and tongue, letting the child feel the vibration of his throat with their fingertips and then feel their own. Step by step, a deaf child who had never heard a word could learn to produce sounds and syllables. It was slow, patient work, and it trained Bell to think about speech in extraordinary detail: exactly how each sound is shaped, and exactly what kind of vibration it makes. That knowledge would turn out to be his secret weapon as an inventor.

In October 1872 he opened his own small school in Boston, which he called a School of Vocal Physiology, to train teachers of deaf students. Vocal physiology means the science of how the body makes the voice. Around 1872–73 he also became a professor of vocal physiology at Boston University's School of Oratory (sources differ on the exact year), while still only in his mid-twenties. He was a tall, dark-haired man with a beard, who often worked late into the night and slept late into the morning.

Teaching was also how Bell met the two families who would change his life. One of his private pupils was a deaf boy named Georgie Sanders. Georgie's father, Thomas Sanders, was a wealthy leather merchant. Bell lived for a time at the home of Georgie's grandmother in Salem, Massachusetts, teaching the boy, and he was allowed to use the basement for his experiments.

Another student, starting in 1873, was a 15-year-old girl named Mabel Hubbard. Mabel had been born on 25 November 1857 in Cambridge, Massachusetts. When she was about five, she caught scarlet fever, a dangerous illness in those days, and it left her completely deaf. Her family refused to send her away to an institution. Instead they helped her learn to speak and to lip-read, and she became extremely good at both, even in several languages. Mabel's father, Gardiner Greene Hubbard, was a Boston lawyer and businessman who helped found the Clarke School for the Deaf in Northampton, the first school in the United States to teach deaf children mainly through speech and lip-reading.

Bell's teaching came from his family's belief that deaf children should be helped to speak and lip-read. In later parts of this Deep Dive we will look at how many Deaf people disagreed with his views, especially about sign language. But in the 1870s he was a dedicated, hard-working teacher, and his students were very important to him. Over time, his feelings for Mabel grew into love. Mabel was more than ten years younger, and her parents at first thought she was too young. In November 1875 the two became engaged, and they married on 11 July 1877.

sections.heading: Backers, a Real Ear and the Mechanic from Salem
paragraphs: Even while teaching full time, Bell spent his evenings on inventions. Like Elisha Gray, he was working on a harmonic telegraph, the multi-message telegraph that used tuned reeds, which you met in Part 5. He even liked to show a party trick: singing a note into a piano and listening to the matching string answer, the same resonance his telegraph depended on.

Inventing costs money, and Bell had little. Two men stepped in. One was Thomas Sanders, Georgie's father. The other was Gardiner Greene Hubbard, Mabel's father. Hubbard had a special interest in the telegraph. He believed Western Union had too much power and had campaigned for the government to run a cheaper postal telegraph service. A system that let one wire carry many messages could shake up the whole telegraph business. In early 1875 the three men made an agreement: Sanders and Hubbard would pay for experiments, and they would share in any patents Bell received.

Bell's mind kept wandering, though, from telegraphs toward speech. In 1874, with the help of a Boston ear doctor, Clarence Blake, he experimented with an amazing and slightly spooky instrument: a real human ear taken from a person who had died, used for medical science. Bell attached a stalk of straw to the tiny bones of the ear. When he spoke into it, the eardrum vibrated, the bones moved, and the straw traced wavy lines on a piece of smoked glass, drawing a picture of his voice. Bell was struck by something. The eardrum was thin and delicate, yet it could move the much heavier bones. Maybe a thin iron disc vibrated by the voice could move enough to change an electric current.

That summer, in July 1874, Bell was back at his parents' home near Brantford. Sitting in his dreaming place above the Grand River, he worked out the principle of a speaking telephone in his head: a sound wave could be copied into an electric current whose strength rose and fell exactly like the air pressure of the voice, and an electromagnet at the other end could turn that current back into sound. Parks Canada's plaque at the Bell Homestead says that the basic idea of the telephone was conceived there in July 1874. Bell would later say the telephone was conceived in Brantford and born in Boston. Knowing the idea and building it, however, were very different things.

Bell was a brilliant thinker about sound, but he was not skilled at building electrical equipment. Fortunately, there was a place in Boston full of people who were. Charles Williams Jr. ran an electrical workshop at 109 Court Street, where inventors went to have their gadgets built. There Bell met a young man named Thomas Augustus Watson. Watson was born on 18 January 1854 in Salem, Massachusetts. He left school as a teenager, tried several jobs, and at 18 joined Williams's shop, where he learned to make telegraph instruments and fire-alarm equipment. Within two years he was one of the most skilled workers there. In 1874 he was assigned to build parts for Bell, and the two quickly became a team. Watson was practical, patient and good with his hands, and Bell was full of ideas. They worked in a room at the top of the building.

In March 1875 Bell visited Washington, D.C., to meet Joseph Henry, the famous American scientist who had built powerful electromagnets decades earlier and was now head of the Smithsonian Institution. Bell explained his ideas, including his hope of sending speech, and admitted he did not know enough about electricity to do it. According to Bell, Henry told him he had the germ of a great invention, and answered his worry with two words: "Get it!" Bell went back to Boston determined.

sections.heading: The Twang of 2 June 1875
paragraphs: Hubbard and Sanders wanted results on the harmonic telegraph, the invention they believed would make money. So through the spring of 1875, Bell and Watson worked on it. Their setup had several transmitters in one room and receivers in another, each with a thin steel reed held over an electromagnet. Normally, each transmitter reed vibrated and rapidly opened and closed a contact, sending a pulsing, on-off current down the wire.

2 June 1875 was a hot day in Boston. Watson was in one room tending the transmitters and Bell was in another room with the receivers. One of Watson's reeds was not vibrating properly. It seemed stuck, and its contact had been screwed down too tightly, so it was not opening and closing the circuit as it should. Watson plucked the reed with his finger to free it.

In the other room, Bell heard something through his receiver: not a plain buzz, but a twang, a sound with the richness of a plucked string, overtones and all. He rushed into Watson's room shouting to ask what he had just done and told him not to change anything.

Why was this so important? Because the contact was stuck closed, the reed was not switching the current on and off. Instead, the vibrating steel reed was moving back and forth near the electromagnet, and a moving magnetized piece of iron near a coil makes a small electric current, the effect Michael Faraday discovered in 1831. That current did not jump between on and off. It rose and fell smoothly, following every detail of the reed's vibration, including its overtones. This was exactly the undulating current Bell had been dreaming about. It proved that a vibrating piece of metal could create a current with the full shape of a sound, and that the current could make another piece of metal vibrate with the same shape far away. Voices are just more complicated vibrations. If a reed could do it, a thin disc moved by the voice should be able to do it too.

Bell described the discovery in letters, and years later he and Watson both told the story many times, with small differences in the details, which is normal for memories. That same evening, Bell sketched a design, and Watson built it, apparently by the next day: a frame shaped like a gallows holding a stretched membrane with a piece of metal attached, over an electromagnet. When Bell spoke or sang into it, Watson, listening at the other end, heard voice-like sounds, but he could not make out clear words. It was progress, but it was not yet a telephone you could talk on.

Over the following months, the two men kept testing. The problem was power. In the gallows design, all the electrical energy came from the speaker's voice moving a bit of metal near a magnet, and a voice does not carry much energy. The current that reached the far end was extremely weak. Bell and Watson tried different membranes, different magnets and different coils. Listening at the receiving end meant pressing an ear tight against the instrument and straining to catch anything at all. They were close, and they knew it, but turning a faint mumble into clear words would take more invention.

sections.heading: Racing Toward the Patent Office
paragraphs: For the rest of 1875 Bell was pulled in many directions. Hubbard pushed him to finish the harmonic telegraph and worried that the speech idea was a distraction. Bell was also teaching, falling in love with Mabel, and, during the summer of 1875 at his parents' home in Brantford, writing out the detailed description of his method that he hoped to patent. He believed his key discovery was not one particular gadget but the principle itself: transmitting sound by an electric current that varies in strength exactly as the air vibrates.

A patent, as our glossary explains, is a government document that gives an inventor the right to control an invention for a set time. In those days, getting a patent in one country first could sometimes cause problems getting one in another. Bell wanted protection in Britain too, and he arranged for a Canadian friend of his family, the politician and newspaper publisher George Brown, to take his description to Britain, so he delayed filing in the United States. But the weeks went by and nothing came of it.

Meanwhile, just as you read in Part 5, Elisha Gray in Chicago was thinking along similar lines. Inventors with similar knowledge, reading the same science and chasing the same telegraph prize, often reach similar ideas at almost the same time. So the question was no longer just who could build a talking machine, but whose ideas would be officially recorded first.

By early 1876 Hubbard had lost patience. Bell was about to hurry his idea toward the patent office in Washington, D.C. He did not know it yet, but on the very same day his application arrived, a lawyer for Elisha Gray would also deliver to that same patent office a description of Gray's own idea for sending speech along a wire.

deepDive: Bell's breakthrough of 2 June 1875 is best understood as the difference between modulating a current by interruption and generating or modulating it continuously. In the harmonic telegraph, a reed driven by its electromagnet opened and closed a contact, producing a pulsed current at the reed's frequency. When the contact screw was set too tightly, the circuit stayed closed, and the plucked reed acted instead as a tiny generator: a magnetized steel reed moving near a coil changes the magnetic flux through the coil, and by Faraday's law of induction this induces a voltage proportional to the rate of change of that flux. The resulting current is analog: its waveform follows the mechanical vibration, overtones included. Bell's existing interest in Helmholtz's analysis of vowels as combinations of harmonics told him why this mattered: if the full waveform could survive, so could the overtones that distinguish speech sounds. The magneto design that grew from this was reversible, the same kind of instrument could act as transmitter or receiver, but its output was tiny, because all the energy came from the voice itself. That is why the gallows prototype produced only faint, unclear sounds, and why later transmitters used a battery whose current was varied by the voice (first a liquid variable-resistance transmitter, then carbon). Historians debate several points about this period. One is how much Bell understood electricity versus how much Watson's craft and Williams's workshop supplied, since Bell himself told Joseph Henry he lacked electrical knowledge. Another is how independent the paths of Bell and Gray were; both were trying to multiplex telegraph lines using tuned reeds, and both moved toward speech within months of each other. A third concerns dates and memories: many famous details, like Henry's "Get it!", come from Bell's own later accounts and testimony in patent cases, where people had reasons to stress particular dates. Notebooks, letters and witness testimony are therefore read carefully, and small disagreements between Bell's and Watson's descriptions of the June experiment are treated as ordinary differences in memory rather than evidence of invention.
funFact: As a teenager, Bell trained his family's Skye terrier to growl while he shaped its mouth with his hands, and he later remembered that the dog could be made to say something like "How are you, Grandmamma?"

check.q: What happened on 2 June 1875 that gave Bell his key clue?
check.a: Watson plucked a stuck reed and Bell heard its twang, with overtones, through the wire in another room
wrong: Bell spoke the first full sentence over a telephone to Watson
